newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Construction firms seen offering returns.
newsitem.headline: Construction firms seen offering returns.

text.p: Hong Kong's current building boom has provided a favourable environment for construction businesses to launch IPOs, with building projects expected to offer promising returns in coming years, analysts said.

"The outlook for the construction sector is expected to be bright in coming years due to local infrastructure development and because many public and private housing projects are on the way," said Kinson Au, senior analyst at PW Asia Brokerage.

With the upturn in the industry, Shui On Construction and Materials Ltd has decided to seek a public listing. The company is a member of the Shui On Holdings Ltd group, which delisted its construction arm Shui On Contractors in 1990.

"The timing is favourable and we see a bright future in the industry because we expect many government housing projects to come up," said Frankie Wong, vice chairman at Shui On Construction and Materials.

The company is offering 65 million shares at HK$9.30 per share in an initial public offering (IPO) launched on January 22. Of the total, 48.75 million shares were offered to professional investors and 16.25 million shares to the Hong Kong public. The offer closes on January 27 and the stock is due to begin trading on February 3.

Construction and property concern Soundwill Holdings Ltd is also expected to launch an IPO in February. Details of the listing are not yet available, but market sources said Soundwill seeking to raise about HK$600 million.

"In view of the improved economy in Hong Kong and China, after the relaxation of austerity measures (in China) last year, it is a good time for a new listing like Shui On," said Ben Kwong, director of research of Dharmala Securities.

Shui On's public listing comes at the start of a big upswing in government building activity. According to the company's listing prospectus, 27 new public works projects will be offered for tender in the first five months of 1997, compared with a total of 27 projects in both 1996 and 1995.
Some analysts, however, expressed concern about competition in the construction industry.
"Competition among construction companies is still a concern, so the strength and capability of the company to tender for both public housing and private (sector) projects is vital," Kwong said.
Construction companies generally compete through the tender process, and this can push margins down to very low levels, analysts said.
"Due to generally low profit margins, there is need for the companies to secure more projects so as to maintain their earnings," said Kelvin Tang, an analyst at Impac Asset Management (HK) Ltd.
Analysts said the construction materials business offered better investment prospects than the construction sector, due chiefly to the fact that there are fewer competitors.
"The construction materials business is considered even more promising due to the fact there are fewer competitors, and that will enhance their longer term earnings prospects," said Kwong.
